message.content:
**Logistic regression** is a statistical method used to model the relationship between one or more predictor variables and a binary (two‑class) outcome. Instead of predicting a continuous value, it predicts the probability that the outcome belongs to a particular class. ### Key features | Feature | Description | |---------|-------------| | **Outcome** | Binary (e.g., 0/1, yes/no, success/failure). | | **Model form** | Uses the logistic (sigmoid) function to map a linear combination of predictors to a probability between 0 and 1:
\(\displaystyle P(Y=1|X)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-(\beta_0+\beta_1X_1+\dots+\beta_pX_p)}}\) | | **Link function** | Logit link: \(\text{logit}(P)=\ln\!\big(\frac{P}{1-P}\big)=\beta_0+\beta_1X_1+\dots+\beta_pX_p\). | | **Estimation** | Parameters \(\beta\) are estimated by **maximum likelihood estimation (MLE)**. | | **Interpretation** | Coefficients represent the change in the log‑odds of the outcome per unit change in the predictor. Exponentiating a coefficient gives an odds ratio. | | **Assumptions** |
  • Independence of observations.
  • Linearity of the logit (predictors linearly related to log‑odds).
  • No perfect multicollinearity.
| | **Extensions** | • **Multinomial logistic regression** for multi‑class outcomes.
• **Ordinal logistic regression** for ordered categorical outcomes.
• **Regularized logistic regression** (L1/L2 penalties) to handle high‑dimensional data. | ### Why use logistic regression? | Reason | Explanation | |--------|-------------| | **Interpretability** | Coefficients can be translated into odds ratios, making it easy to explain the effect of each predictor. | | **Probabilistic output** | Provides estimated probabilities, useful for risk scoring or decision thresholds. | | **Computational efficiency** | Relatively fast to fit even on large datasets. | | **Baseline model** | Often used as a baseline for comparison with more complex classifiers. | ### Example Suppose we want to predict whether a patient has a disease (1) or not (0) based on age and blood pressure: \[ \text{logit}(P) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{Age} + \beta_2 \times \text{BP} \] After fitting the model, we might obtain: - \(\beta_0 = -5.0\) - \(\beta_1 = 0.04\) (each additional year of age increases log‑odds by 0.04) - \(\beta_2 = 0.02\) (each additional mmHg of BP increases log‑odds by 0.02) For a 60‑year‑old patient with BP 140: \[ \text{logit}(P) = -5.0 + 0.04(60) + 0.02(140) = 0.8 \] \[ P = \frac{1}{1+e^{-0.8}} \approx 0.69 \] So the model estimates a 69 % probability of disease. --- **In short:** Logistic regression is a simple yet powerful tool for binary classification that models the probability of an event using a logistic function applied to a linear combination of predictors.
